title: Rust: Generics
description: Use generic type parameters to write reusable, type-safe code in Rust.

steps.title: Generic Function
steps.description: Write a generic function `identity<T>(value: T) -> T` that returns the value unchanged. Test with i32 42 and &str "hello".

steps.title: Generic Struct
steps.description: Define a generic struct `Pair<T, U>` with fields `first: T` and `second: U`. Implement a method `first(&self) -> &T`. Create a Pair<i32, &str> and print both fields.
hints: `struct Pair<T, U> { first: T, second: U }`
Method: `impl<T, U> Pair<T, U> { fn first(&self) -> &T { &self.first } }`

steps.title: Generic with Trait Bound
steps.description: Write a generic function `largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T` that returns the largest element in a slice. Test with i32 and &str slices.
hints: Iterate and compare: `if item > largest { largest = item }`

steps.title: Generic Enum (Option-like)
steps.description: Define a generic enum `MyOption<T>` with variants `MySome(T)` and `MyNone`. Implement a method `is_some(&self) -> bool`. Create and test both variants.
hints: `impl<T> MyOption<T> { fn is_some(&self) -> bool { matches!(self, MyOption::MySome(_)) } }`
This is how Rust's built-in `Option<T>` works!

verification.failureMessage: Create MySome(42) and MyNone and call is_some() on each.

steps.title: Generic Associated Function
steps.description: Add an associated function `new(first: T, second: U) -> Self` to the Pair struct that creates a new Pair. Also add a `swap` method that returns Pair<U, T>.
hints: `fn new(first: T, second: U) -> Self { Self { first, second } }`
`fn swap(self) -> Pair<U, T> { Pair { first: self.second, second: self.first } }`
Generic methods can have additional type parameters.

verification.failureMessage: Create Pair::new(42, "hello"), swap it, and print both fields.
